description: A vigorous annual climbing vine with soft hairy leaves, nocturnal white flowers, and smooth pale-green cylindrical or bottle-shaped fruits prized for cooling summer dishes.
identifying_features: Vigorous twining tendril-bearing vine with soft, velvet-hairy musk-scented stems
Broad, heart-shaped (cordate) or kidney-shaped leaves with shallow lobes and wavy margins
Solitary, nocturnal white flowers with crinkled petals opening late afternoon
Smooth, pale-green fruits in cylindrical, club, or dumbbell shapes with white spongy flesh and flat seeds
habitat: Alluvial agricultural fields, village roof trellises, and home garden pergolas.
distribution: Native to tropical Africa and South Asia; cultivated throughout India for thousands of years.
uses: Light, cooling staple vegetable cooked into Lauki ki Sabzi, Lauki Kofta, Lauki Kheer, and Bengali Lau Ghonto
Fresh juice consumed as an Ayurvedic cooling health tonic and digestive aid TODO(verify)
Dried, hollowed woody gourds historically crafted into the soundbox resonator of the sitar, tanpura, and rudra veena
care_tips: Provide a sturdy bamboo arbor, trellis, or rooftop scaffolding to support heavy hanging gourds
Requires full direct sunshine and organically enriched, moisture-retentive loam soil
Water generously and consistently during vine growth and fruit swelling
toxicity_note: WARNING: NORMAL SWEET LAUKI IS SAFE. BITTER BOTTLE GOURD IS EXTREMELY TOXIC: Never consume bottle gourd juice that tastes bitter. Bitter gourds contain high levels of toxic cucurbitacins B and D, which cause acute toxic shock, hematemesis (vomiting blood), gastrointestinal bleeding, and organ failure. Always taste a small raw piece before juicing or cooking; discard immediately if bitter.
fun_fact: Dried, hollowed bottle gourds were among the world's very first domesticated containers and floating water jugs, carried across oceans by early human navigators over 10,000 years ago.

description: A vigorous creeping or climbing vine with large mottled leaves, bright golden-orange bell-shaped blossoms, and heavy ribbed fruits with nutrient-dense, sweet orange flesh.
identifying_features: Extensive trailing or climbing vine with angled stems and branched tendrils
Large, soft, dark green heart-shaped leaves often patterned with silver-white blotches at vein intersections
Large, showy bright yellow-orange flared trumpet flowers (edible blossoms)
Large variable fruit (globose, flattened, or oblong) with ribbed rind and thick, sweet orange flesh enclosing flat seeds
habitat: Farmland fields, river sandbanks (diara farming), and home compost beds.
distribution: Native to Mesoamerica and South America; universally cultivated throughout India as a staple vegetable.
uses: Cooked into sweet-and-sour Kaddu ki Sabzi, Bengali Kumror Chhokka, and sambar stews
Nutrient-dense seeds (magaz) roasted as healthy snacks or ground into festive sweet gravies
Rich dietary source of beta-carotene (provitamin A), lutein, and potassium
care_tips: Requires vast ground area or heavy-duty arbors to support rambling 5-10 meter vines
Thrives in hot, sunny weather and loose, fertile soil enriched with aged cow manure
Mulch soil beneath developing fruits with straw to prevent rot from ground moisture
toxicity_note: Non-toxic; flesh, blossoms, tender leaves, and seeds are completely edible and safe for humans and pets.
fun_fact: In Bengali cuisine, practically zero waste is generated from pumpkin: the flesh, tender climbing shoot tips (kumro shaak), yellow flowers (kumro phul bhaja), and seeds are all prized delicacies.

description: A fast-growing rough-stemmed annual climbing vine bearing small yellow flowers and crisp, cooling cylindrical green fruits containing over 95% water.
identifying_features: Slender climbing or trailing vine with rough bristly stems and unbranched coiled tendrils
Rough, triangular-ovate palmately 3-5 lobed leaves with acute lobes
Small yellow star-like flowers in leaf axils (separate male and female flowers)
Elongated cylindrical green fruits with warty or smooth skin and pale crisp seed-filled juicy flesh
habitat: Riverbed sands, alluvial vegetable farms, polyhouses, and home garden trellises.
distribution: Native to the foothills of the Himalayas in India; cultivated across the world for over 3,000 years.
uses: Essential cooling raw salad vegetable eaten fresh with lemon juice and chaat masala, or folded into boondi raita
Natural hydrator containing over 95% water, electrolytes, and silica
Chilled slices placed over eyes to reduce puffiness and soothe tired skin
care_tips: Trellis vines vertically to keep cucumbers clean, straight, and well-aerated
Requires consistent, deep watering; moisture stress produces bitter, misshapen fruits
Harvest cucumbers while crisp and firm before seeds enlarge and skins turn yellow
toxicity_note: Safe and wholesome; occasional bitter cucumbers contain elevated cucurbitacins (usually concentrated near the stem end) and should be trimmed or discarded.
fun_fact: Ancient Sanskrit texts mention cucumber cultivation under the name 'Trapusha' over three millennia ago, confirming India as the original botanical homeland of the global cucumber.

description: A low-growing legume herb renowned for its remarkable habit of geocarpy, where pollinated flower stems bend downward and drill beneath the soil to develop underground pods.
identifying_features: Low, bushy, or sprawling annual legume reaching 30-50 cm in height
Pinnate leaves with four broad, obovate leaflets arranged in two opposite pairs
Bright yellow pea-like flowers blooming low on stems; after pollination, the floral stalk ('peg') elongates downward and burrows into the soil
Reticulated woody underground pods containing 1 to 4 oil-rich edible seeds covered in thin reddish-brown papery seed coats
habitat: Sandy loam agricultural plains, light well-drained soils, and semi-arid cropping belts.
distribution: Native to South America; extensively cultivated across western and southern India (Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu).
uses: Roasted, salted, or boiled as iconic winter street snacks (moongphali) across Indian railway stations and markets
Major commercial source of groundnut oil, the preferred traditional cooking oil of Gujarat and Maharashtra
High natural source of plant protein, healthy monounsaturated fats, resveratrol, and Vitamin E
care_tips: Requires light, loose, sandy loam soil so emerging pegs can easily penetrate underground
Thrives in warm, sunny weather; sensitive to soil compaction and waterlogging
Keep soil loose around the base of plants during flowering and pegging stages
toxicity_note: Non-toxic; peanuts are one of the most common severe food allergens, capable of triggering life-threatening anaphylaxis in allergic individuals. Ensure peanuts are stored dry to avoid toxic aflatoxin mold.
fun_fact: Peanuts are not true nuts at all, but botanical legumes related to peas and beans, famous for their unique habit of flowering in the air and ripening their pods underground.

description: A tall, erect annual bast-fiber herb celebrated as the source of 'The Golden Fiber', with slender stalks that yield strong, silky, biodegradable natural fibers after retting.
identifying_features: Tall, straight, slender unbranched annual herb reaching 2 to 4 meters in height
Alternate, ovate-to-lanceolate leaves with serrated margins, characterized by two hair-like tail bristles at the base of the blade
Small, bright yellow 5-petaled flowers borne solitary or in pairs in leaf axils
Elongated, ribbed cylindrical 10-angled seed capsules containing numerous small grayish seeds
habitat: Alluvial floodplains, water-rich river basins, and monsoon-inundated delta soils.
distribution: Native to the Indian subcontinent and tropical Africa; Bengal (India and Bangladesh) is the global epicentre of jute production.
uses: Bast fibers woven into burlap, gunny sacks, twine, eco-friendly shopping bags, and geo-textiles ('The Golden Fiber')
Tender mucilaginous young leaves cooked as a prized nutritious green potherb (Pat shaak) in Bengal and Egypt (Molokhia)
Completely biodegradable, eco-friendly alternative to synthetic plastic packaging materials
care_tips: Requires high temperatures, high monsoon humidity, and deep, standing alluvial silt soils
Grown during the monsoon season when rainfall is abundant
Retting: harvested stalks must be submerged in slow-flowing fresh water for 2-3 weeks to soften and strip fibers
toxicity_note: Tender young leaves are a safe, edible vegetable; mature seeds contain cardiac glycosides (olitoriside) and should not be consumed TODO(verify).
fun_fact: Jute is the second most important natural vegetable fiber in the world after cotton, and is celebrated as 'The Golden Fiber' for its natural golden sheen and vital economic importance.

description: An evergreen climbing tropical vine ubiquitously grown in Indian households in jars of water and hanging baskets, prized for its glossy heart-shaped variegated leaves and feng shui prosperity symbolism.
identifying_features: Trailing or climbing vine with adventitious aerial roots that grip supports or flourish directly in standing water
Glossy, heart-shaped (cordate) juvenile leaves marbled with vibrant splashes of yellow, cream, or lime-green
In wild mature forest conditions, leaves become gigantic (up to 1 m long) with deep pinnatifid leaf splits
Almost never flowers in domestic cultivation due to a genetic deficiency in gibberellin synthesis
habitat: Indoor living rooms, balconies, office corridors, and tropical tree trunks.
distribution: Native to Mo'orea in French Polynesia; universally cultivated across India and worldwide as an indestructible houseplant.
uses: Popular Vastu Shastra and Feng Shui houseplant believed to attract wealth, prosperity, and positive energy
Top-rated indoor air-purifying plant shown to remove indoor toxins including formaldehyde, benzene, and xylene
Versatile ornamental grown in soil pots, moss poles, or simple glass bottles filled with water
care_tips: Thrives in bright indirect light; tolerates low-light conditions (though variegation fades in deep shade)
Allow the top 2 inches of soil to dry out between waterings; avoid soggy, anaerobic soil
If growing in water jars, change the water every 7-10 days to maintain oxygenation and prevent algae
toxicity_note: TOXIC TO PETS AND CHILDREN: Contains insoluble needle-shaped calcium oxalate crystals (raphides). Chewing any part causes immediate intense burning and stinging of the mouth, tongue, and lips, excessive drooling, difficulty swallowing, and vomiting in cats, dogs, and humans.
fun_fact: Golden Pothos earned the nickname 'Devil's Ivy' because it is nearly impossible to kill and stays vibrantly green even when neglected in windowless dark corners.

description: An architectural, virtually indestructible succulent herb with erect, sword-like stiff leaves banded with wavy grey-green horizontal patterns and golden borders.
identifying_features: Dense basal clusters of rigid, erect, vertical sword-shaped succulent leaves growing 0.5 to 1.5 m tall
Distinctive horizontal wavy zigzag banding of light and dark olive-green resembling snakeskin, often with bright yellow margins
Tough, fibrous underground rhizomes that creep and push up new pups
Slender spikes of greenish-white tubular nocturnal flowers emitting a light sweet fragrance in mature plants
habitat: Dry tropical rocky forests, shaded arid bushlands, and modern indoor living spaces.
distribution: Native to tropical West Africa; grown everywhere globally and across India as a durable indoor plant.
uses: Renowned NASA Clean Air Study plant that converts CO2 into oxygen at night via Crassulacean Acid Metabolism (CAM)
Filters airborne toxins including benzene, formaldehyde, trichloroethylene, and xylene
Architectural focal point for modern minimalist interior design and drought-tolerant rock gardens
care_tips: Water sparingly; allow soil to dry out completely between waterings; overwatering causes fatal root rot
Tolerates full blazing sun as well as low-light indoor corners
Use well-aerated cactus or succulent potting soil with perlite and pumice
toxicity_note: MILD-TO-MODERATE TOXICITY: Foliage contains saponins. Ingestion by cats and dogs causes excessive salivation, vomiting, nausea, diarrhea, and lethargy.
fun_fact: Unlike most houseplants that release oxygen only during daytime photosynthesis, the Snake Plant performs CAM photosynthesis, releasing oxygen throughout the night, making it ideal for bedrooms.

description: A graceful, easy-care clump-forming indoor perennial with arching ribbon-like variegated leaves and long wiry runners bearing miniature plantlets ('spiderettes').
identifying_features: Dense rosette of arching, linear, ribbon-like leaves up to 30-45 cm long, striped with green and creamy-white margins or centers
Long, wiry, yellowish arching stolons (runners) extending 60-90 cm outward
Small, starry, six-petaled white flowers borne along the runners
Miniature tufted plantlets with nascent aerial rootlets dangling from runners like spiders on a web
habitat: Coastal riverine forests, rocky forest floors, and residential hanging baskets.
distribution: Native to tropical and southern Africa; widely popular throughout India as a hanging terrace and indoor basket plant.
uses: Classic hanging basket and shelf ornamental with cascading tiers of dangling plantlets
Highly effective natural air purifier removing carbon monoxide, formaldehyde, and airborne dust particles
Safe, non-toxic pet-friendly indoor houseplant
care_tips: Provide bright, indirect sunlight; direct midday sun scorches and bleaches the tender ribbon leaves
Keep soil evenly moist in spring and summer; water when top inch of soil feels dry
Snip off dangling spiderettes and root them in moist soil or water for effortless propagation
toxicity_note: NON-TOXIC: Completely safe for cats, dogs, and children. Cats are often attracted to spider plants because they contain mild compounds with a mild hallucinogenic/catnip-like effect on felines, though it is physically harmless.
fun_fact: A single healthy mother Spider Plant can produce dozens of dangling baby plantlets simultaneously on its arching stolons, giving rise to its common name 'Hen and Chickens'.

description: An iconic tropical climbing hemiepiphyte renowned for its enormous, glossy, perforated and deeply split emerald-green leaves and stout aerial cord roots.
identifying_features: Massive climbing vine with stout stems producing thick, cord-like brownish aerial roots
Huge, glossy, heart-shaped leathery leaves that develop dramatic natural perforations (fenestrations) and deep splits
Creamy-white boat-shaped spathe enclosing a stout spadix that develops into an edible cob-like fruit
Fruit covered in hexagonal green scales that pop off naturally when fully ripe to reveal sweet pineapple-banana pulp
habitat: Tropical rainforest understory, climbing up mature host trees, and stylish interior spaces.
distribution: Native to tropical rainforests of southern Mexico to Panama; massively popular across India as a premium indoor statement plant.
uses: Premier architectural statement plant featured in contemporary interior design and boutique hotels
Naturally removes indoor airborne pollutants and enriches ambient room humidity
Ripe fruit (ceriman) is eaten as a rare delicacy tasting of a hybrid between pineapple, banana, and mango
care_tips: Place in bright indirect or filtered sunlight; harsh direct sun bleaches and burns the glossy leaves
Provide a sturdy moss pole, coir totem, or trellis for aerial roots to climb
Water thoroughly when the top 2-3 inches of soil dry; wipe dust off broad leaves with a damp cloth
toxicity_note: FOLIAGE AND UNRIPE FRUIT ARE TOXIC: All vegetative parts contain sharp needle-like insoluble calcium oxalate crystals (raphides). Chewing foliage causes intense oral burning, swelling of tongue and throat, and digestive distress in pets and humans. Only the completely ripe fruit (whose outer green scales fall off voluntarily) is edible.
fun_fact: The natural holes in Monstera leaves are called 'fenestrations' (from the Latin for window); they allow hurricane winds to pass through without tearing the leaf and let sunlight filter down to lower foliage.

description: An elegant, shade-tolerant evergreen perennial herb with glossy lanceolate leaves and striking, pure-white hood-like floral spathes that resemble white flags of peace.
identifying_features: Dense, stemless clumps of arching, glossy dark green elliptic leaves with sunken veins
Pure snow-white, petal-like oval spathes emerging above the foliage on slender erect stalks
Central, creamy-yellow cylindrical spadix covered in tiny true flowers
Dramatic wilting behavior ('fainting') when thirsty, followed by rapid full recovery within hours of watering
habitat: Dense tropical rainforest understory floors, shaded riverbanks, and dimly lit home interiors.
distribution: Native to tropical rainforests of Central and South America; universally cultivated as an indoor decorative houseplant.
uses: Celebrated as a symbol of peace, purity, and healing, frequently gifted during housewarmings and milestones
One of the top-performing houseplants for removing benzene, formaldehyde, carbon monoxide, and toluene from indoor air
Thrives in low-light indoor spaces where few other flowering plants can survive
care_tips: Prefers medium to low indirect light; direct sunshine will scorch the leaves and brown the white spathes
Keep potting soil consistently moist but never soggy; water as soon as leaves begin to gently droop
Wipe broad leaves periodically to remove dust and maintain high photosynthetic efficiency
toxicity_note: TOXIC TO DOGS AND CATS: Contains insoluble calcium oxalate crystals. Ingestion causes immediate oral pain, burning of lips and tongue, drooling, difficulty swallowing, and vomiting. Keep out of reach of domestic pets.
fun_fact: The white 'flower' of the Peace Lily is not a true flower at all, but a modified leaf called a spathe that serves as a protective hood and billboard to guide pollinators to the tiny true flowers on the spadix.

description: A magnificent banyan-group evergreen tree native to Northeast India, famous for its colossal buttressed roots, living root bridges of Meghalaya, and thick, glossy, leathery oval leaves.
identifying_features: Massive forest tree developing vast buttresses and aerial prop roots in humid wild habitats
Large, thick, leathery, glossy oblong-oval leaves up to 20-35 cm long with a prominent pinkish-red midrib
Emerging new leaves tightly enclosed in a bright crimson-red or pinkish stipular sheath that drops as the leaf unfurls
Copious thick milky white latex sap exuding immediately from any broken leaf or stem
habitat: Humid subtropical rainforests, river ravines of Meghalaya and Assam, and domestic indoor pots.
distribution: Native to Northeast India (Meghalaya, Assam), Myanmar, and Indonesia; grown worldwide as a popular houseplant.
uses: Aerial roots trained by the indigenous Khasi and Jaintia tribes of Meghalaya to create centuries-old, living root bridges across roaring rivers
Historical source of natural rubber latex before the Amazonian rubber tree (Hevea brasiliensis) became dominant
Bold, dramatic indoor specimen plant prized for its shiny architectural foliage
care_tips: Thrives in bright, indirect sunlight; can tolerate gentle morning direct sun
Water thoroughly when the top two inches of potting mix feel dry; reduce watering during winter months
Clean leaves with a soft damp cloth to keep the glossy surface free of dust and mineral deposits
toxicity_note: MILD-TO-MODERATE TOXICITY: The milky latex contains ficin and psoralens. Contact with skin or eyes causes irritation and dermatitis; ingestion can cause vomiting, drooling, and mouth irritation in dogs and cats.
fun_fact: The incredible Living Root Bridges of Meghalaya, some carrying foot traffic for over 500 years, are meticulously grown and woven by indigenous Khasi villagers using the living aerial roots of Ficus elastica.

description: A charming, long-lived woody-stemmed succulent with fleshy, teardrop-shaped jade-green leaves, revered in Feng Shui as a symbol of financial wealth, good fortune, and renewal.
identifying_features: Thick, gnarled, miniature tree-like woody branching trunk giving it a natural bonsai appearance
Fleshy, plump, glossy jade-green oval or obovate opposite leaves, often developing red margins in bright sun
Clusters of tiny, delicate, star-shaped white or pale-pink flowers in late winter or early spring
Extremely durable succulent foliage capable of storing water for months of drought
habitat: Rocky arid scrub hills, succulent valleys, and sunny indoor balcony planters.
distribution: Native to KwaZulu-Natal and the Eastern Cape of South Africa; universally popular as an ornamental and feng shui plant across India.
uses: Premier Feng Shui and Vastu houseplant placed near home or office entrances to attract financial prosperity and harmony
Ideal living bonsai specimen that naturally develops an ancient, thick-trunked appearance with minimal training
Drought-resilient tabletop succulent requiring minimal maintenance
care_tips: Requires at least 4-6 hours of bright direct or filtered sunlight; insufficient light causes leggy, drooping stems
Water thoroughly only when the soil has dried out completely; highly vulnerable to stem rot from overwatering
Plant in porous, gritty succulent/cactus potting mix with perlite or pumice
toxicity_note: TOXIC TO CATS AND DOGS: Ingestion by pets causes vomiting, depression, ataxia (unsteady gait), and slow heart rate. Keep placed on high shelves away from household pets.
fun_fact: Jade plants can live for over 70 to 100 years, often passed down through multiple family generations as living family heirlooms.

description: A robust, drought-conquering succulent cactus composed of flattened paddle-like green stem segments (cladodes), yellow blossoms, and sweet, juicy, spine-armed oval fruits.
identifying_features: Segmented succulent shrub formed of thick, flattened, obovate green pad-like stem joints (cladodes)
Pads armed with clusters of minute, barbed hair-like bristles (glochids) and occasional sharp spines
Large, cup-shaped bright golden-yellow or orange flowers opening on the upper margins of terminal pads
Ovoid, fleshy berry fruits (tunas) ripening from green to ruby-red or purplish-crimson with sweet juicy seed-filled pulp
habitat: Arid deserts, dry rocky wastelands, semi-arid agricultural field boundaries, and saline scrublands.
distribution: Native to Mexico; naturalized extensively across arid and semi-arid regions of western and peninsular India.
uses: Nutritious sweet fruit (tunas / prickly pears) peeled and eaten fresh, rich in betalain antioxidants and Vitamin C
Tender young pads (nopales) cleaned of spines and grilled or cooked in traditional Mexican cuisine
Formidable living barbed security fence planted along rural agricultural borders to exclude cattle and wild boars
care_tips: Requires full, blazing, intense direct sunshine and hot temperatures
Needs sharply draining sandy, gravelly, or rocky soil; immediately rots in waterlogged conditions
Extremely drought tolerant; requires virtually no supplemental watering once established
toxicity_note: Fruit flesh and pads are non-toxic and edible. MECHANICAL IRRITATION HAZARD: The tiny microscopic hair-like barbed spines (glochids) easily detach and penetrate skin or mucous membranes, causing persistent severe mechanical dermatitis, itching, and pain. Handle only with thick leather gloves or tongs.
fun_fact: Prickly pear cladodes are the traditional host plant for cochineal insects (Dactylopius coccus), the historic source of natural carmine red dye used to color royal fabrics, cosmetics, and foods.

description: A lush, arching graceful fern with long, feathery sword-shaped fronds bearing alternating pinnate leaflets, beloved worldwide as a classic hanging porch and indoor bathroom fern.
identifying_features: Gracefully arching, pendulous pinnate fronds up to 0.5 to 1.5 meters long emerging from a central tufted crown
Alternate, closely spaced triangular-oblong leaflets (pinnae) with slightly serrated or wavy margins
Underground creeping rhizomes and thin fibrous runners producing daughter plantlets
Two neat rows of rounded spore-bearing sori protected by kidney-shaped indusia along the underside of fertile pinnae
habitat: Damp tropical swamps, humid shaded rock crevices, epiphytic on tree trunks, and indoor hanging pots.
distribution: Native to tropical forests of the Americas, West Indies, and Polynesia; universally cultivated across India.
uses: Quintessential hanging basket fern bringing lush, arching woodland greenery to verandas, living rooms, and patios
Outstanding natural humidifier and air purifier capable of absorbing indoor formaldehyde and xylene
Safe, non-toxic plant for households with dogs and cats
care_tips: Requires high atmospheric humidity; mist regularly or place in naturally humid bathrooms or kitchens
Provide bright, dappled indirect light; avoid harsh direct sun which bleaches and browns frond tips
Keep potting soil consistently moist but well-drained; never allow the root ball to dry out completely
toxicity_note: NON-TOXIC: Completely safe and non-toxic for cats, dogs, birds, and children.
fun_fact: The popular Boston Fern originated in 1894 when a Massachusetts florist noticed a spontaneous mutation with wider, more gracefully arching and ruffled fronds among a shipment of wild sword ferns.

description: A stunning, shade-tolerant tropical foliage herb renowned for its lush, spear-shaped leaves beautifully patterned in silver, grey, pink, and vibrant ruby-red variegation.
identifying_features: Compact, erect clumping herbaceous stems reaching 30 to 80 cm in height
Broad, elliptic-lanceolate leathery leaves with striking silver-grey feathering or vivid pink/red splashes along primary veins
Greenish-white arum-like floral spathes enclosing a pale spadix, followed occasionally by red ornamental berries
habitat: Tropical rainforest understories, shaded humid damp slopes, and low-light home interiors.
distribution: Native to the tropical rainforests of the Philippines and Sulawesi; widely grown across India as an elite indoor accent plant.
uses: Celebrated as one of the best and easiest indoor houseplants for low-light apartments and offices
Top-tier air-cleansing houseplant documented in NASA studies for filtering toxins like benzene and formaldehyde
Provides vibrant color accents indoors through contemporary pink and red cultivars (e.g., 'Siam Aurora')
care_tips: Thrives in low to bright indirect light; keep entirely shielded from hot direct sun
Allow the top 2 inches of soil to dry before watering again; highly susceptible to root rot if overwatered
Keep away from cold air conditioners and drafty doorways; prefers temperatures above 16°C
toxicity_note: TOXIC TO PETS AND CHILDREN: Contains insoluble needle-like calcium oxalate crystals. Chewing any part causes immediate intense burning and swelling of the mouth, tongue, and throat, excessive drooling, and digestive distress.
fun_fact: In China and throughout East Asia, Aglaonema has been cultivated for centuries as an auspicious good-luck plant believed to bring good fortune, prosperity, and positive chi into the home.
